summary: Explains why weak or predictable random number generators are a serious risk for TLS and similar security protocols, and describes a way for implementations to harden their randomness. The idea is to mix a long-term private key into the random generator's inputs, so that output stays unpredictable even if the system's entropy source is weak.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8937 hardens the random numbers a security protocol uses. The idea is to mix in something the attacker does not have, namely a signature made with the party's own long-term private key, and to derive the random values from the result. That way a broken random number generator does not automatically give up the key.

questions: why is randomness important for tls
how to improve random number generation in security protocols
subtitle: Mixing a long-term private key into the random number generator so its output stays unpredictable even if the generator is broken.

tldr.problem: Protocols such as TLS depend on the system random number generator being good, and a broken or deliberately weakened generator leaks the keys it was used to protect.
tldr.mechanism: Instead of using the generator's output directly, the RFC derives a key from it together with a signature over a fixed tag made with the party's long-term private key, and expands the requested randomness from that key.
tldr.outcome: The output still looks random if the generator is sound, and it still looks random if the generator is fully controlled by an attacker, provided the private key stays secret. The private key only has to be reachable through a signing operation, so it can stay inside a hardware security module.

facts.label: Signature over the fixed tag
facts.value: Computed once for the lifetime of the wrapper

today: RFC 8937 is an Informational document from October 2020 representing the consensus of the Crypto Forum Research Group. No RFC obsoletes or updates it, so it stands as the description of the PRF randomness wrapper and the conditions under which it holds.

sections.title: Why Wrap the Random Number Generator
sections.content:
A secure and properly implemented random number generator, or a cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator (CSPRNG), should produce output that is indistinguishable from a random string of the same length. CSPRNGs are critical building blocks for TLS and related transport security protocols. TLS in particular uses them to generate several values, such as ephemeral key shares and the ClientHello and ServerHello random values. CSPRNG failures, such as the Debian bug, can lead to insecure TLS connections, and CSPRNGs may also be intentionally weakened to cause harm. Initial entropy sources can also be weak or broken, which would lead to insecurity of all CSPRNG instances seeded with them. Where CSPRNGs are poorly implemented or insecure, an adversary may be able to distinguish their output from a random string or predict it, and recover the secret key material used to protect the connection.

The document proposes an improvement inspired by the NAXOS trick. Instead of using raw randomness where needed, for example in generating ephemeral key shares, a function of a party's long-term private key is mixed into the entropy pool. In the NAXOS key exchange protocol the raw random value x is replaced by H(x, sk), where sk is the sender's private key. The difficulty is that private keys are often isolated in Hardware Security Modules, so direct access to compute H(x, sk) is impossible, and some HSM APIs may only offer the option of signing messages with a private key, with no other operation involving that key. An alternate but functionally equivalent construction is needed.

The approach replaces the NAXOS hash with a keyed hash, or pseudorandom function, where the key is derived from a raw random value and a private key signature. Implementations SHOULD apply the technique when indirect access to a private key is available and CSPRNG randomness guarantees are dubious, or to provide stronger guarantees about possible future issues with the randomness.

The security properties the construction provides are roughly these. If the CSPRNG works fine, that is, its output is indistinguishable from a truly random sequence in a certain adversary model, then the output of the proposed construction is also indistinguishable from a truly random sequence in that model. An adversary with full control of a potentially broken CSPRNG and the ability to observe all outputs of the construction does not obtain any non-negligible advantage in leaking the private key, in the absence of side channel attacks. And if the CSPRNG is broken or controlled by the adversary, the output of the construction remains indistinguishable from random, provided that the private key remains unknown to the adversary. The document represents the consensus of the Crypto Forum Research Group.
sections.plainLanguage: When the random numbers a protocol uses can be predicted, the attacker gets the session keys with them, and a long-term key can follow. The fix here is to derive the random values from two things: what the generator produced, and a signature made with the server's own private key. The attacker can break the first but not the second, so the output stays unpredictable.

sections.title: The Randomness Wrapper
sections.content:
The output of a properly instantiated CSPRNG should be indistinguishable from a random string of the same length, but this is not always true. To mitigate the problem, the document proposes wrapping the CSPRNG output with a construction that mixes secret data into a value that may be lacking randomness.

Let G(n) be an algorithm that generates n random bytes, the output of a CSPRNG. Define an augmented CSPRNG G' as follows. Let Sig(sk, m) be a function that computes a signature of message m given private key sk. Let H be a cryptographic hash function producing output of length M. Let Extract(salt, IKM) be a randomness extraction function, such as HKDF-Extract, which accepts a salt and an input keying material parameter and produces a pseudorandom key of L bytes suitable for cryptographic use; it must be a secure PRF, with the salt as a key of length M, and must preserve the uniformness of the input keying material. L SHOULD be a fixed length. Let Expand(k, info, n) be a variable-length output PRF, such as HKDF-Expand, taking a pseudorandom key k of L bytes, an info string and an output length n, and producing n bytes. Finally, let tag1 be a fixed, context-dependent string, and tag2 a dynamically changing string, such as a counter, of L' bytes. The construction requires that L is at least n minus L' for each value of tag2.

Instead of using G(n) when randomness is needed, use G'(n), where G'(n) = Expand(Extract(H(Sig(sk, tag1)), G(L)), tag2, n). Functionally, this expands n random bytes from a key derived from the CSPRNG output and a signature over a fixed string. Expand() generates a string that is computationally indistinguishable from a truly random string of n bytes, so the security of the construction depends on the secrecy of H(Sig(sk, tag1)) and of G(L). If the signature is leaked, the security of G'(n) reduces to the case where randomness is expanded directly from G(L).

If a private key is stored and used inside an HSM, the signature calculation is implemented inside it, while all other operations, including the hash function, the Extract function and the Expand function, can be implemented either inside or outside the HSM. Sig(sk, tag1) need only be computed once for the lifetime of the randomness wrapper and MUST NOT be used or exposed beyond its role in that computation.

Sig MUST be a deterministic signature function, such as deterministic ECDSA, or use an independent and completely reliable entropy source, for example when it is implemented in an HSM with its own internal trusted entropy source for signature generation. Because Sig(sk, tag1) can be cached, the relative cost of using G'(n) instead of G(n) tends to be negligible with respect to cryptographic operations in protocols such as TLS, where the comparatively inexpensive cost of HKDF-Extract and HKDF-Expand dominates. The values of G'(n) may also be precomputed and pooled, since the construction depends only on the CSPRNG output and the private key.
sections.plainLanguage: The wrapper takes two inputs, the random bytes from the system generator and a signature over a fixed tag made with the long-term key. It mixes them with HKDF-Extract, then stretches the result with HKDF-Expand to the length the caller asked for. Because the signature can be computed once and cached, the extra cost is small, and because only a signing operation is needed, the private key never has to leave the hardware module that holds it.

sections.title: Tag Generation
sections.content:
Both tags MUST be generated so that they never collide with another contender or owner of the private key. This can happen, for example, if one HSM holding a private key is used from several servers, or if virtual machines are cloned.

The recommended construction is as follows. tag1 is a constant string bound to a specific device and protocol in use, which allows Sig(sk, tag1) to be cached. Device-specific information may include, for example, a Media Access Control address. To provide security where CSPRNGs are used in virtual environments, it is RECOMMENDED to incorporate all available information specific to the process that would ensure the uniqueness of each tag1 value among different instances of virtual machines, including ones that were cloned or recovered from snapshots. This is needed to address the problem of CSPRNG state cloning. If the private key could be used for other purposes, choosing a value for tag1 that differs from the form allowed by those other uses ensures that the signature is not exposed.

tag2 is a nonce, that is, a value that is unique for each use of the same combination of G(L), tag1 and sk values. It can be implemented using a counter or a timer, provided the timer is guaranteed to differ for each invocation of G'(n).
sections.plainLanguage: Two strings keep the construction safe. The first is fixed per device and protocol and says which key is being used, so that a signature made for one purpose is never seen by another. The second changes every time, so that two calls with the same key never produce the same output. The first must include whatever makes the machine unique, because a copied virtual machine would otherwise produce identical values.

sections.title: Applying It to TLS and Getting It Right
sections.content:
The PRF randomness wrapper can be applied to any protocol in which a party has a long-term private key and also generates randomness, which is true of most TLS servers. To apply it to TLS, one simply replaces the private CSPRNG G(n), the CSPRNG that generates private values such as key shares, with G'(n) = HKDF-Expand(HKDF-Extract(H(Sig(sk, tag1)), G(L)), tag2, n).

For implementation, the wrapper requires L to be at least n minus L', where L is the Extract output length and n is the desired amount of randomness. Some applications may require n to exceed this bound, and wrapper implementations can support that case by invoking G' multiple times and concatenating the results.
sections.plainLanguage: For TLS the change is one substitution: wherever the server would have used its own random generator for a secret value, it uses the wrapper instead. The only wrinkle is length. The key derived from the generator and the signature has a fixed size, so asking for more randomness than that key can supply means calling the wrapper more than once and joining the results.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A security analysis was performed elsewhere, and the following theorem has been proven: if the adversary learns only one of the signature or the usual randomness generated on one particular instance, then, under the security assumptions on the primitives, the wrapper construction should output randomness that is indistinguishable from a random string.

The main reason one might expect the signature to be exposed is a side-channel attack. It is therefore prudent when implementing this construction to take into consideration the extra long-term key operation if equipment is used in a hostile environment, and it is recommended to generate a key specifically for the purposes of the defined construction and not to use it in any other way.

The signature in the construction, as well as in the protocol itself, MUST NOT use randomness from entropy sources with dubious security guarantees. The signature scheme MUST either use a reliable entropy source, independent of the CSPRNG being improved, or be deterministic. If the signatures are probabilistic and use weak entropy, the construction does not help, and the signatures remain vulnerable to repeat randomness attacks, in which the adversary might recover the long-term key used in the signature.

Under these conditions, applying this construction should never yield worse security guarantees than not applying it, assuming that applying the PRF does not reduce entropy. The construction is generic, so the analyses of many protocols will still hold even if it is incorporated.

The construction cannot provide any guarantees of security if the CSPRNG state is cloned due to virtual machine snapshots or process forking. It is RECOMMENDED that tag1 incorporate all available information about the environment, such as process attributes and virtual machine user information.
sections.plainLanguage: Two conditions have to hold for the scheme to work. The signature must be made in a way that does not itself depend on weak randomness, so it has to be deterministic or use a separate good source. And the whole scheme fails if the generator's internal state has been copied, which is why the fixed tag should carry everything that makes the machine distinct.

sections.title: Comparison to RFC 6979
sections.content:
The construction has similarities with RFC 6979, since both use private keys to seed a deterministic random number generator. Section 3.3 of RFC 6979 recommends deterministically instantiating an instance of the HMAC_DRBG pseudorandom number generator, using the private key sk as the entropy_input parameter and H(m) as the nonce. The construction G'(n) given here is similar, with the difference that a key derived from G(n) and H(Sig(sk, tag1)) is used as the entropy input and tag2 is the nonce.

The semantics and the security properties obtained from using the two constructions are different. The construction proposed here aims to improve CSPRNG usage such that certain trusted randomness remains even if the CSPRNG is completely broken. Using a signature scheme that requires entropy sources, as RFC 6979 intends, is for different purposes and does not assume possession of any entropy source, even an unstable one. For example, if in a certain system all private key operations are performed within an HSM, the HMAC_DRBG construction described in RFC 6979 may be implemented inside the HSM for the sake of signature generation, while the construction proposed here assumes calling the signature implemented in the HSM.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 6979 also uses a private key to seed a generator, but for a different job: making a signature deterministic so it needs no randomness of its own. This RFC works the other way round, taking whatever randomness the system generator produces and adding the private key to it, so that a failure of the generator alone is not enough to predict the protocol's secrets.

data.title: The randomness wrapper
data.code:
G'(n) = Expand(Extract(H(Sig(sk, tag1)), G(L)), tag2, n)

and, for TLS:

G'(n) = HKDF-Expand(HKDF-Extract(H(Sig(sk, tag1)), G(L)), tag2, n)

with the requirement  L >= n - L'  for each value of tag2.

items.title: A sound generator stays sound
items.text: If the CSPRNG output is indistinguishable from random, the output of the wrapper is too.

items.title: A broken generator does not leak the key
items.text: An adversary with full control of the CSPRNG and who sees every output gains no non-negligible advantage in recovering the private key, in the absence of side channel attacks.

items.title: A broken generator still looks random
items.text: If the CSPRNG is broken or controlled, the output stays indistinguishable from random, provided the private key remains unknown.
